# Joshua 24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## v. 1 — The Assembly at Shechem

Joshua gathers all Israel's tribes to Shechem, a site of profound covenant history. Abraham first built an altar to Yahweh there after receiving the land promise (Gen 12:6–7); Jacob buried his household idols there (Gen 35:4) and built an altar calling it "El Elohe Israel" (Gen 33:18–20). The valley between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim formed a natural amphitheater where Joshua had earlier read the law with its blessings and curses (Josh 8:30–35). Constable notes that Shechem was to Israel what Plymouth Rock, Yorktown, Lexington, and Independence Hall combined would be to Americans. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

The four leadership categories (elders, heads, judges, officers) recur from Joshua 8:33 and 23:2; their exact distinctions are uncertain. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

The phrase "presented themselves before God" raises the question of where the tabernacle was. Some (e.g., Bush, cited in Precept Austin) suggest the tabernacle was temporarily moved from Shiloh to Shechem for this occasion. Others note the Septuagint reads "Shiloh" in v. 1 and v. 25, possibly an attempt to resolve the difficulty. Bush argues for the Shechem reading, citing the historic appropriateness and the fact that Shechem was a Levitical city closer to Joshua's home at Timnath-serah. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-24-commentary)

David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/Charismatic) highlights that Shechem's acoustics made it ideal for addressing large crowds. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

---

## v. 2 — The Prophetic Word Begins: Idolatrous Origins

Joshua speaks as a prophet: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel." God begins His historical review not with Abraham's greatness but with the family's pagan origins beyond the Euphrates. Terah, Abraham, and Nahor "served other gods." Ur and Haran were centers of moon worship (Schaeffer, cited by Guzik). The point is grace: God chose Abraham from a pagan, idolatrous home. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Ellicott notes that "flood" (KJV) here means "river" — the Euphrates. He observes that this speech was addressed to all the people (not just rulers as in ch. 23), including many "of but little thought and education, whom it was necessary to inform and remind." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/24.htm)

Dr. Bob Utley (bible.org) notes that Terah's name itself may reflect moon worship. Abraham was not chosen for his theology or merit; God's choice was pure grace. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## vv. 3–4 — Abraham to the Patriarchs

God took Abraham from beyond the Euphrates, led him through Canaan, multiplied his descendants, and gave him Isaac. To Isaac, God gave Jacob and Esau; Esau received Mount Seir, while Jacob and his sons went to Egypt.

Utley notes the verb "gave" (nātan) appears three times in these verses, emphasizing YHWH's power, control, and eternal purposes. Mount Seir refers to the land south of the Dead Sea, usually associated with Edom. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

Guzik notes that God's summary of history remarkably omits all Israel's sin and rebellion — reflecting the promise of Jeremiah 31:34 that God will "remember their sin no more." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

---

## vv. 5–7a — The Exodus and Red Sea

God sent Moses and Aaron, plagued Egypt, and brought Israel out. At the Red Sea, when the Egyptians pursued with chariots and horsemen, Israel cried out and God put darkness between the camps, then brought the sea upon the Egyptians. God emphasizes: "Your very eyes saw what I did."

Guzik notes that the "darkness" (v. 7) was the same cloud that was darkness to Egypt but light to Israel (Exod 14:19–20) — a manifestation of God's presence that simultaneously judged and protected. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Utley similarly observes that the darkness cloud represented YHWH's presence: darkness to the Egyptians, light to the Israelites. The Hebrew word (BDB 66) is the same used for the ninth plague. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## vv. 7b–10 — The Wilderness and Transjordan Conquests

God summarizes the wilderness period with remarkable brevity: "Then you lived in the wilderness for a long time." Guzik again notes the striking omission of Israel's sin — God "forgot" their rebellion in this recounting. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

God brought them into the land of the Amorites east of the Jordan, delivering those kings into their hand.

Verses 9–10 recall Balak king of Moab hiring Balaam to curse Israel, but God would not listen to Balaam — instead Balaam "blessed you again and again." Constable notes that Balak's war was spiritual in nature (Numbers 22–25); it was fought through curses and seduction, not swords. The UBS Translators Handbook (cited by Utley) notes "fought against Israel" seems to contradict Numbers 22:6,11 and Deuteronomy 2:9, suggesting it may mean "prepared to fight" or "opposed." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

Utley notes the Hebrew construction for "bless" (Piel imperfect + Piel infinitive absolute of bārak) expresses intensification: Balaam had to keep on blessing. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## vv. 11–13 — Conquest of Canaan and Undeserved Blessing

God recounts the crossing of the Jordan, the battle for Jericho, and victory over the seven Canaanite nations. Verse 12 mentions "the hornet" sent ahead to drive out the two Amorite kings — something God did, "not by your own sword or bow."

Constable identifies the "hornet" as "various hornet-like terrors" God used to rout Israel's enemies (cf. Exod 23:28; Deut 7:20). Utley calls it "possibly a metaphor of divine activity causing fear" since it is mentioned but never narrated as a literal event. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

Verse 13 is a summary of grace: Israel enjoys land they did not toil for, cities they did not build, vineyards and olive groves they did not plant. Constable notes the implied warning: those who planted these were removed by God's righteous judgment, and Israel could suffer the same fate. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

**Covenant Structure Note:** Constable and Utley both observe that Joshua 24 follows the structure of a Hittite suzerainty treaty from the second millennium BC: preamble (v. 1–2a), historical prologue (vv. 2b–13), stipulations with consequences (vv. 14–24), and deposit of the treaty document (vv. 25–28). This parallel supports the early dating of the material. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html) (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## v. 14 — "Fear the LORD and Serve Him in Sincerity"

Joshua draws the "now therefore" conclusion from God's mighty acts: fear the LORD, serve Him in sincerity and truth, put away the foreign gods, and serve the LORD.

Guzik, following Francis Schaeffer, observes that the three bodies of water in the historical review (Euphrates, Red Sea, Jordan) correspond to three sets of false gods: the gods of heritage (Sumerian/Babylonian), the gods of upbringing (Egyptian), and the gods of the surrounding culture (Amorite/Canaanite). Joshua's point: the LORD is greater than all of them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Utley notes this verse contains a series of Qal and Hiphil imperatives. The phrase "sincerity and truth" focuses on inner attitude and outer lifestyle (cf. Deut 6:4–5). "Truth" (ʾĕmet) is the OT root for faith/believe/trust. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## v. 15 — "As for Me and My House, We Will Serve the LORD"

This is among the most famous verses in the OT. Joshua presents a genuine choice: if serving the LORD seems undesirable, then choose — the gods of Mesopotamia (heritage) or the gods of the Amorites (current culture). But Joshua declares his own settled decision: "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

**Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic)** emphasizes the Hebrew tense: it expresses continuous action — "I have chosen, and I will choose." Joshua could say this because he had a lifetime of continuous faithfulness: fighting Amalekites, rejecting the golden calf, serving Moses humbly, trusting God against the majority report. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

**John Piper (Baptist/Reformed, Desiring God)** preaches that Joshua's declaration models the duty of family worship. Even at over 100 years old, with death approaching, Joshua was confident his influence would continue so that his household would keep serving the LORD. Piper stresses that the word "serve" here can be translated "worship" — making family worship the application. Joshua addressed the heads of households (v. 1) and declared what he wanted every household to do. Piper notes Joshua 24:31 shows Joshua's influence pervaded Israel for a generation because it was grounded in family worship. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/leading-family-worship)

Piper also warns that Joshua 24:22–23 shows that choosing to serve God can coexist with a heart far from Him — hence the command to "incline your heart." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/is-joy-a-choice-or-a-feeling)

**Spurgeon (Baptist)** preached a sermon titled "Decision — Illustrated by the Case of Joshua" from this text, emphasizing resolute personal decision regardless of what others do. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/decision-illustrated-by-the-case-of-joshua)

**Ellicott** observes that Joshua pledges his "house" though no descendant of Joshua is named anywhere in the Bible (1 Chron 7:27 lists Joshua as the last in his line). He finds this "profoundly significant" as an analogy with Christ: "whose house are we, if we hold fast" (Heb 3:6). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/24.htm)

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** emphasizes that Joshua spoke as head of his house for all his household — "This is as it should be with all Christian men today (Ephesians 6:4)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-24.html)

---

## vv. 16–18 — The People's Response

The people recoil at the idea of forsaking the LORD. They recite God's mighty acts: the Exodus from Egypt, the great signs, His protection throughout their journey, and His driving out the Canaanites. They conclude: "We too will serve the LORD, for He is our God!"

Guzik notes that their declaration was based on God's past dealings with them — how could they not serve such a great God? (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Ellicott observes that "the feelings of the people are naturally shocked by the bare mention of apostasy. They will not forsake Jehovah on any account. But their answer only betrayed their want of intelligence. They missed the point of Joshua's argument, as may be seen by his reply." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/24.htm)

---

## vv. 19–20 — "You Cannot Serve the LORD"

Joshua's startling reply: "You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God; He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins." If they forsake Him for foreign gods, He will bring disaster and consume them.

**Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Joshua is not discouraging faith but discouraging superficial commitment. Jesus did the same when He demanded total commitment (Luke 14:25–33). Joshua wanted the people to understand that serving God under the Mosaic covenant meant they would be cursed for disobedience. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

**Constable:** Israel would "not be able to serve the Lord" in their own strength by sheer determination. God is holy and jealous (allowing no rival). "He will not forgive your transgressions or your sins" means He will not spare when transgression is willful and forgiveness would lead to no amendment (citing Lange). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

**Ellicott:** "Jehovah will not consent to be served as one God among many — the very thing which Israel was doing at the moment, which they meant to do, and did do, with rare intervals, down to the Babylonish captivity." Israel always maintained Jehovah as national deity but also recognized other national deities, thinking it necessary to propitiate them. Joshua's argument was "perfectly intelligible, and was entirely necessary for those times." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/24.htm)

**Utley:** This follows the revelation to Moses in Deut 31:16–22. "Holy God" is plural in Hebrew (plural of majesty), intensifying the concept. "Jealous God" is a love word implying deep personal relationship (as father or husband). The phrase about not forgiving refers to covenant rebellion — God will not overlook willful apostasy (cf. Exod 23:21). This highlights "the problem of the first covenant — fallen human inability to maintain fellowship with a holy God." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

**Ligonier (Reformed):** A Ligonier devotional on this passage clarifies that "no general rule is laid down [for all sin], but the discourse is directed, as often elsewhere, against their disobedient temper. It does not refer to faults in general, or to special faults, but is confined to gross denial of" the faith — i.e., apostasy. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joshua-farewell)

---

## v. 21 — "No! We Will Serve the LORD!"

Despite the severe warning, the people insist: "No, but we will serve the LORD." Ellicott: "Being brought to the point, no other answer was possible. If they must give up Jehovah or the idols, the idols must go first." Guzik: this was the response Joshua wanted — a commitment made with full understanding. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

---

## vv. 22–24 — Witnesses and Practical Obedience

Joshua declares them witnesses against themselves. Then he calls for immediate action: "get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD." The people respond with a third affirmation.

Guzik notes that Joshua immediately called them to act on their words. Citing Adam Clarke: "A man's promise to serve God soon loses its moral hold of his conscience if he do not instantaneously begin to put it in practice." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Ellicott observes a sober note: "we do not read that they did anything in obedience to these words. We read of no images being buried or burned...There is only a verbal promise." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/24.htm)

Utley notes "put away foreign gods" suggests the gods were already in their midst — likely Canaanite household gods. Amos 5:27 seems to confirm this. The second half ("incline your hearts") implies attitudes, not just objects. Yet 1 Kings 8:58 says it is YHWH who must cause hearts to incline — the human responsibility and divine sovereignty stand together. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## vv. 25–27 — The Covenant and Its Memorials

Joshua "made a covenant" — not a new covenant but a renewal of the Mosaic covenant. Constable distinguishes "statute" (the written commitment to obey the law) from "ordinance" (the record of blessings for obedience). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

Joshua wrote "these words" in the Book of the Law of God. Ellicott notes this is "the second signature among the sacred writers of the OT." Moses was the first (Deut 31:9), Samuel the next (1 Sam 10:25). "They did not look upon themselves as writers of distinct books, but as authorised to add their part to the book already written...The unity of Holy Scripture is thus seen to have been an essential feature of the Bible from the very first." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/24.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary adds: Joshua recorded "not the whole history of his campaigns...but the public ratification of the Mosaic covenant which had now been made. This he added to his copy of the book of the law." It explains how later additions (like the account of Moses' death in Deuteronomy) follow this same principle. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/24-26.htm)

The large stone set under the oak near "the sanctuary of the LORD" is a permanent witness. Constable says the sanctuary is "this holy place" (Shechem itself, consecrated by patriarchal history), not the tabernacle at Shiloh. The oak may be the same tree where Jacob buried his household idols (Gen 35:4) and near where Abraham first built his altar (Gen 12:6–7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

Guizik notes that the stone and the people together form the two witnesses required by Deut 19:15 for a binding covenant. The personification of the stone ("it has heard all the words") was a common rhetorical device. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Utley confirms this personification was characteristic of Hittite treaties, where natural objects (rocks, trees, mountains) served as witnesses. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## v. 28 — Dismissal

Joshua sends the people away, each to his inheritance. A simple transitional verse closing the covenant ceremony.

---

## vv. 29–31 — The Death of Joshua

Joshua dies at 110 — the same age as Joseph (Gen 50:26). Utley suggests this age may have been symbolic of a blessed life. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

Guzik notes that the title "servant of the LORD" was used often of Moses but only here of Joshua — a high honor. Joshua was buried in his inheritance at Timnath-serah in Ephraim. There seemed to be no great state funeral; his epitaph is simply "the servant of the LORD." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

Verse 31 testifies that Israel served the LORD throughout Joshua's lifetime and the lifetime of the elders who outlived him — those who had personally "experienced all the works that the LORD had done." Constable calls this "a common theme in the OT" — those who experienced God's power remained faithful, but the next generation often went astray (cf. Judges). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

Utley adds: "Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua...This is a common theme in the OT. Those who experienced YHWH's power and deliverance remained faithful, but the next generation which only heard about it often went astray (e.g., the book of Judges)." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

---

## v. 32 — The Burial of Joseph's Bones

Joseph's bones, brought from Egypt (Gen 50:24–26; Exod 13:19), are finally buried at Shechem on the plot Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor for one hundred pieces of silver (Gen 33:19). This land became part of the inheritance of Joseph's descendants (Ephraim and Manasseh).

Constable calls this a testimony to God's faithfulness: Joseph had counted on God's promise and now, centuries later, it was fulfilled. The three burials ending the book — Joshua, Joseph, Eleazar — all testify that "God kept His word." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

The Pulpit Commentary and Precept Austin mention the possibility that this burial occurred at the same covenant assembly, adding weight to the choice of Shechem. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-24-commentary)

---

## v. 33 — The Death of Eleazar

Eleazar son of Aaron, the high priest throughout Joshua's leadership, also dies and is buried at Gibeah (a site in Ephraim given to his son Phinehas).

Constable: "As Israel's high priest he was more important than the brief references to his ministry might suggest." The three graves — Joshua, Joseph, Eleazar — all rest within the Promised Land, demonstrating God's faithfulness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html)

Gill (cited in the brief biblehub excerpt) notes a Jewish tradition that Eleazar's burial by Phinehas is recorded in the chapter. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/24.htm)

---

## Denominational Distinctives

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasizes that this is a covenant renewal ceremony following the pattern of God's sovereign grace. The historical prologue (vv. 2–13) focuses entirely on what God has done, not what Israel did. The warnings of vv. 19–20 are interpreted as directed specifically against the "disobedient temper" of gross apostasy, not all sin generally. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joshua-farewell)

**Baptist (Piper/Desiring God; Spurgeon):** Draws from v. 15 the duty of family worship and the father's responsibility as spiritual head of the household. Piper emphasizes that "serve" can be translated "worship" and that Joshua's influence, rooted in family worship, pervaded the nation for a generation. Spurgeon preached personal, resolute decision regardless of what others choose. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/leading-family-worship)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasizes the Hebrew continuous-action tense in v. 15 ("I have chosen and I will choose"), highlighting Joshua's lifelong pattern of Spirit-empowered obedience. Guzik also stresses the need for immediate practical action following verbal commitment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-24/)

---

## Modern Scholarship

**Hittite Suzerainty Treaty Parallel:** Both Constable (StudyLight) and Utley (bible.org) detail the parallel between Joshua 24 and second-millennium BC Hittite treaty forms: preamble → historical prologue → stipulations → blessings/curses → witnesses → document deposition. This is seen as evidence for the early dating and essential unity of the material. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-24.html) (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

**The "Hornet" (v. 12):** Multiple scholars (Constable, Utley) treat the hornet as a metaphor for divine terror or panic, not a literal insect plague, since it is never narrated as an event elsewhere. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)

**The Stone as Witness (v. 27):** Personification of natural objects as covenant witnesses is a recognized feature of ancient Near Eastern treaty forms. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/joshua-24)
